c.tagline: Japan's most storied hot-spring town, steaming beside the Yubatake

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are clean, safe, and expensive by distance; most visitors get around on foot or by the town's onsen loop bus instead.

emergency.note: 119 covers both ambulance and fire; some English support is available on emergency lines in this tourist area.

hood_desc: The steaming, sulfur-scented heart of town, built around the wooden troughs of the Yubatake where hot spring water cascades and glows at night; ryokan, shops, and foot baths ring the square.
A wooded park a short walk uphill from the center, with free open-air baths tucked among the trees and a peaceful, forested atmosphere away from the main crowds.
A quieter residential onsen district with small local bathhouses used more by residents than tourists, offering an everyday, unpolished side of the town.
The main shopping street lined with souvenir shops, izakaya, and the Netsu-no-Yu bathhouse, where staff perform the traditional 'yumomi' water-cooling dance.
The edge of town where the road climbs toward Mt. Kusatsu-Shirane's volcanic crater lake, popular for hiking and ropeway views in warmer months.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink; hot-spring water is for bathing only.

transit.pay: cash or IC card on board
transit.map: available at the tourist information center near the Yubatake
transit.note: The town center is compact and walkable; the loop bus mainly helps reach outlying ryokan and the ropeway.

air: No local airport; nearest is Tokyo Haneda (HND)
train: JR Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi Station, then a 25-minute connecting bus into town
bus: Direct highway buses run from Tokyo (Shinjuku/Ikebukuro), about 4 hours

tip.r: Tipping is not practiced and can cause confusion; excellent service is simply the norm, included in the price.

food.name: Onsen tamago
food.desc: Eggs slow-cooked in mineral hot-spring water until the white is barely set and the yolk is custardy, eaten from the shell with a splash of dashi soy.

places.name: Yoritomo
places.note: A pickle shop whose onsen tamago has a strong local reputation; sold to eat on the spot.

places.name: Shops along Yubatake-dori
places.note: Several counters around the steaming hot-water field sell them warm in pairs, all day.

places.name: Stalls near Sainokawara Park
places.note: Convenient snack on the walk up to the open-air rotenburo bath.

food.name: Onsen manju
food.desc: Small steamed buns of brown-sugar dough filled with sweet red bean paste, made with the mineral water of Mount Kusatsu-Shirane and eaten warm.

places.name: Matsumuraya Manju
places.note: Famous for handing out free samples with tea to passers-by; buns are steamed through the day.

places.name: Honke Chichiya
places.note: One of the long-established Kusatsu manju makers, with boxed sets for taking home.

places.name: Shops along Yubatake-dori
places.note: A dozen competing manju shops line the main street, so it is easy to compare.

food.name: Age-manju
food.desc: Onsen manju rolled in tempura batter with black sesame and deep-fried to order, crisp outside and molten inside; the town's guiltiest street snack.

places.name: Matsumuraya Manju
places.note: Fries them fresh on request, so you get them hot rather than sitting under a lamp.

places.name: Snack stalls on Yubatake-dori
places.note: Sold on a stick for easy eating while walking the steaming main street.

places.name: Shops near Kusatsu Onsen bus terminal
places.note: Last chance to grab one before the bus back to Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi.

food.name: Handmade soba
food.desc: Buckwheat noodles cut by hand and served cold on a bamboo mat with dipping broth, or hot in a clear soup; a Gunma highland staple.

places.name: Mikuni Soba
places.note: The town's best-known soba shop, with queues at lunch; go early or late.

places.name: Kisoba Ushidaitei
places.note: Handmade soba and udon, popular with residents as well as visitors.

places.name: Soba Hanashigara
places.note: Quieter alternative for soba and tempura sets away from the busiest street.

food.name: Sansai tempura
food.desc: Mountain wild vegetables such as fiddlehead fern, butterbur bud and udo, dipped in light batter and fried; a spring speciality of the Gunma highlands.

places.name: Mikuni Soba
places.note: Tempura sets with soba are the standard order, and the wild-vegetable version is seasonal.

places.name: Kisoba Ushidaitei
places.note: Serves tempura alongside its handmade noodles, with local produce in spring.

places.name: Soba Hanashigara
places.note: Reviewers single out the soba and tempura combination here.

food.name: Konnyaku dengaku
food.desc: Gunma is Japan's konjac heartland: firm konnyaku skewered, warmed and painted with sweet miso, sold as a cheap savoury snack between baths.

places.name: Stalls around the Yubatake
places.note: Grilled skewers sold hot beside the steaming water field, a good winter warmer.

places.name: Yoritomo
places.note: Pickle and local-produce shop that also sells konnyaku products to eat or take away.

places.name: Shops near Kusatsu Onsen bus terminal
places.note: Souvenir shops stock packaged Gunma konnyaku alongside ready-to-eat skewers.

food.name: Amazake
food.desc: Thick, sweet, barely alcoholic drink made from fermented rice koji, served steaming in a paper cup with a pinch of ginger on cold mountain evenings.

places.name: Stalls around the Yubatake
places.note: Sold hot beside the illuminated hot-water field, the classic thing to hold after a bath.

places.name: Matsumuraya Manju
places.note: Serves warm drinks with its steamed buns, a natural pairing.

places.name: Cafes near Sainokawara Park
places.note: Rest stops along the walk to the open-air bath serve amazake and tea.

food.name: Gunma jizake (local sake)
food.desc: Sake brewed with Gunma mountain water, mostly dry and clean, drunk warm in winter; many Kusatsu inns pour prefectural labels you will not see elsewhere.

places.name: Izakayas along Yubatake-dori
places.note: Small evening bars near the hot-water field list several Gunma breweries by the glass.

places.name: Kisoba Ushidaitei
places.note: Soba shops traditionally serve sake with the noodles; a good low-key place to try it.

places.name: Liquor shops near Kusatsu Onsen bus terminal
places.note: Stock prefectural labels in small bottles, useful for tasting more than one.

landmarks: Yubatake
The steaming 'hot water field' at the town's heart, where wooden channels cool 4,000 liters of sulfurous spring water per minute beneath rising clouds of vapor.
Netsu-no-yu (Yumomi Show)
A wooden bathhouse theater where kimono-clad performers stir scalding spring water with long paddles in the traditional, song-accompanied yumomi cooling ritual.
Sainokawara Park
A volcanic ravine on the town's edge where emerald hot-spring pools bubble among rocks, leading to one of Japan's largest open-air baths.
Sainokawara Open-Air Bath
A vast 500-square-meter rotenburo at the head of the hot-spring ravine, where bathers soak amid forest scenery that turns magical under winter snow.
Kosenji Temple
A hillside temple overlooking the Yubatake whose 'Yukake Matsuri' blessing and evening bell have watched over Kusatsu's bathers for centuries.
Gozanoyu Bathhouse
A beautifully reconstructed Meiji-style public bath beside the Yubatake, offering wooden and stone tubs fed by two different historic spring sources.
Otakinoyu
A beloved bathhouse famous for awase-yu, a sequence of progressively hotter cedar pools that lets bathers acclimatize to Kusatsu's potent acidic waters.
Shirane Shrine
A quiet forest shrine on a knoll above the town, dedicated to the volcano deity Yamatotakeru and reached by mossy stone steps.
Tenguyama (Kusatsu Onsen Ski Resort)
The town's mountain playground, offering ski runs in winter and lifts, forest walks and family activities through green summer months.
Nishinokawara Park
A quieter hot-spring park on Kusatsu's west side with footbaths, small waterfalls and stone Kannon statues, linking the town to its western bathhouses.

train.note: Japan has no international trains, and Kusatsu Onsen in Gunma has had no railway of its own since the line closed in 1964. The nearest station is Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi on JR East's Agatsuma Line, reached by direct limited express from Ueno in Tokyo in around 2 hours 30 minutes, or by taking the Hokuriku Shinkansen to Takasaki and changing onto the Agatsuma Line. From the station a JR bus climbs to the Kusatsu Onsen Bus Terminal in about 25 minutes. Note this is Kusatsu in Gunma, not the similarly named city in Shiga on the Tokaido Line.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan, but the coach is the most practical way into Kusatsu. JR Bus Kanto (https://www.jrbuskanto.co.jp/) runs direct highway buses from Shinjuku in Tokyo to the Kusatsu Onsen Bus Terminal in about 4 hours, and operates the connecting shuttle up from Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi Station. Seibu Kanko Bus links Kusatsu with Karuizawa in roughly 80 minutes, a scenic mountain route that is closed or diverted in winter. Reserve highway seats online in advance for weekends and the autumn-leaf season.

ferry.note: Kusatsu is a landlocked hot-spring town high in the Gunma mountains, so there are no ferry or boat services of any kind.

half.name: Mount Kusatsu-Shirane and Yugama Crater
half.blurb: An active volcano above town whose milky turquoise crater lake, Yugama, is among the most otherworldly and acidic lakes on Earth.
